author: haiku
reason: A defines every term an outsider would need (ID token, authorization code, Redis, sid, the lockout fields), explains why the design works as it does (matching by sub, skipping the lockout check for a known sub), covers cases that B leaves out (an existing account with no password, an account already linked to this user) and gives the exact schema, so a newcomer can build a complete picture of the system from it.

author: haiku
reason: B is better for a newcomer: it defines terms like OIDC, the authorization code, the ID token and Redis, explains why accounts match by sub and why linking needs a password, and covers cases A leaves open (an existing account with no password, a sub already linked to the same user, how start_session and /login behave, and the migration SQL).

author: sonnet
reason: A explains more for a newcomer: what the existing system looks like (Redis versus PostgreSQL, the start_session internals, the exact lockout rules), why the mechanisms work (the SameSite=Lax cookie on the return, deleting the attempt atomically, how a Google-only user is kept from being locked out), and it states the login-CSRF open question precisely, whereas B is more scannable but thinner and vaguer on those points.

author: sonnet
reason: B is better for someone new to the project: it describes the existing system (the Postgres tables, what Redis is used for, and how start_session and its cookies work), explains state, nonce and PKCE, gives the reasons behind choices such as SameSite=Lax and deleting the pending link on lockout, and lays out the login-CSRF attack step by step, while A is shorter but assumes more prior knowledge.

author: haiku
reason: A is longer, but it defines every term it relies on, explains why the design is safe (the success row commits atomically with the merge, re-runs are idempotent, the lookback is applied once after missed nights), and has a failure table and specific open questions; B is quicker to read but leaves gaps, such as several "see open questions" pointers with no matching question and logging success after the commit rather than inside it.

author: haiku
reason: B is longer, but it explains how the system behaves where A is vague or silent: how equal timestamps are handled (A contradicts itself on this), soft deletes, hung attempts, catch-up after a missed night, when the Sunday reconciliation starts, and a full table of failures, so a newcomer can understand the whole design without guessing.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains why the design is the way it is, for example that `updated_at` is stamped at write time rather than commit time, and why all bookkeeping lives in the warehouse; it also names one owner for retries, crash detection and failure logging, while B leaves crash and attempt counting vague and split between the job, the next attempt and an unnamed paging step.

author: sonnet
reason: B is longer, but it explains why things are the way they are: there is no write access to the app database, and a row's timestamp is set at write time rather than commit time, which is why the 2-hour lookback exists. It also says plainly that the scheduler owns retries, crash detection and the failure rows, which A leaves vague (for example, "the paging step marks it failed"). So B gives someone new to the project a clearer picture of how the system actually works.

author: haiku
reason: B is shorter and gives every step the same layout, and it decides the hard mechanisms (the 8-day replay window, the lowest-offset first-copy rule, the check that live processing has finished the day, the alert thresholds), so I come away with a working picture of the whole system; A defines its terms more patiently but repeats itself and leaves core behaviour, such as how replay finds earlier first copies and how crash recovery works, as open questions.

author: haiku
reason: A gives a newcomer a short, consistent model: every step uses the same layout (trigger, action, data kept, failure), and it explains the parts that aren't obvious, such as why replay reads from D-8 and why the day closes at 02:00. B has a fuller glossary and a failure table, but it is longer and padded, and its replay dedup doesn't match live dedup, which it leaves as an open question.

author: sonnet
reason: A gives an outsider a fuller picture of how the system works: it defines every moving part (acknowledged, raw log partition, duplicate, staging table) and gives the reason behind each mechanism, such as hashing on event_id so all copies of an event share a partition and are deduplicated in order. B is tighter and makes a few sharper decisions, but it leaves more for the reader to infer.

author: sonnet
reason: B is the better document for an outsider to learn the system from: its opening paragraph covers the starting point, the goal and why duplicates and replay exist, and it explains how the parts fit together (all copies of an `event_id` go to the same partition, each worker handles events in order, and failed enrichment is repaired later by replay) where A gives the same steps with less reasoning behind them.

author: haiku
reason: Document A is easier to learn the system from: an up-front summary, terms with concrete limits (512 MB workers, 5 MB parts, 60 s API timeout, 7-day bucket rule) and reasons for each choice, and a failure table give a newcomer the full picture, while B's per-step Starts/Does/Keeps template and its extra robustness logic (owner claim, crash-repair re-enqueue) assume more background and leave out context such as how filters and columns apply to the small-report stream.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to understand: it opens by saying what the export does and why, its glossary explains the limits the design depends on (at-least-once delivery, multipart part sizes, bucket lifecycle rules, payload limits, report sizes), and it adds a failure table and the table schema, even though A is tighter on concurrency (owner claim, crash repair).

author: sonnet
reason: Both are clear, and A states the reason for the small/large split better, but B pairs each step with its own failure handling and explains its ordering choices (it sends the email before setting done, so no user is left without a link). It also covers gaps that A misses, such as replica lag, a record stuck in queued if the API dies before enqueueing, and expired links, which leaves an outsider with a more complete and trustworthy model of how the system behaves.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for an outsider to follow: it says why the small/large split exists (60 s request limit, 512 MB workers), defines row_id, view state, signed URLs and the nightly row_count rewrite (A mentions a "nightly rebuild" it never introduces), and puts the failure cases in one table, though A handles the email-before-done ordering better.

author: haiku
reason: A defines everything a newcomer to the stack needs (Redis, Lua script, atomic, TTL, cache hit) and states each mechanism precisely, such as Redis server time deciding the window and the exact inputs and outputs of check_and_incr; B is easier to scan but assumes more background and adds claims the brief never made.

author: haiku
reason: B is better for a newcomer because it defines the stack terms A takes for granted (Redis, Lua script, TTL, atomic, Key Service, backend), says why each choice was made (one noisy customer, one shared counter across six instances, Redis server time so gateway clocks don't matter), and its failure table shows the response, whether the counter changed, and the metric for each case.

author: sonnet
reason: A defines every term a newcomer would need (customer, plan, Key Service, fail open, TTL), and explains why the key scheme and Redis clock work. It walks through each step and failure mode, including a definite interim rule for Enterprise customers and the Redis timeout case that may or may not have been counted. B is tighter but leaves gaps, such as Enterprise behaviour being undecided, and its diagram has the Key Service returning a customer ID even when the key is unknown.

author: sonnet
reason: B is longer, but for someone new to the project it is the better handover: it defines every term (customer, plan, Key Service, TTL, fail open), explains why a shared Redis and its clock keep the 6 instances in step, says what Enterprise requests get for now, and covers the unclear cases A leaves out (a request whose Redis call times out may or may not have been counted, and a long Redis outage adds up to 50 ms to every request).

author: haiku
reason: A has a separate "how the system runs" section that explains each part (write modes, the copy and its version rule, sweeper, comparer, backfill, switch procedure, IDs, reads) and says why each one works, and it adds a failure table, so a newcomer can build a complete mental model; B is shorter but spreads the mechanism across rollout steps and leaves real gaps, such as an unknown scheduler for the sweep and erased users who can reappear.

author: haiku
reason: B gives a newcomer what A leaves out: the starting facts (row counts, load, the replica's role, what the job system does), definitions of terms like replica lag and StaleWrite, a separate section on how writes, erasures, copies, the sweeper, IDs and reads work in each mode, and a table of failures. That lets a reader understand both why and how the system works, while A's shorter step list assumes context the reader doesn't have.

author: sonnet
reason: A gives a newcomer more of what they need to understand the system: scale figures, why repair uses a durable table instead of the Redis queue, mode names that say which database is primary (dual_mysql/dual_pg), a runtime section covering writes, reads and the sweeper, a timed write-pause budget and a failure table, while B is shorter but leaves more unexplained and backs up MySQL only after the point of no return.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow because it explains its context and reasons: table size and traffic, why the Redis queue is avoided, how replica lag works, and how the freeze's 90-second budget is split. It also lays out the write, read and sweeper flows separately, adds a failure table, and starts with a phase overview. A is compact but leaves out much of the why.

author: haiku
reason: B gives a newcomer a clearer working picture: its diagram draws a separate rollback path for each starting mode, every step lists what starts it, what it does and what data it reads and writes, and it says where state lives. A keeps one path and needs notes to explain which steps are skipped, and it leaves many of the mechanics as "not stated" across more than twenty open questions.

author: haiku
reason: A gives a tighter, more concrete model: its diagram shows each mode's own rollback steps instead of one path corrected by a note, it defines what comparison_results holds and when a mismatch counts as resolved, and every step lists its trigger, data and failure behaviour, while B is longer and buries the mechanism under many "not specified" caveats.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives a newcomer a quicker and sounder mental model: a mode table showing which engine does what, a diagram with each transition's trigger and gate on its arrow, and an explicit charge check plus the ledger's one-charge rule that explain why no mode change, forward or back, can double-charge. A has more precise gate and reconcile detail, but it never explains how forward moves avoid double charging.

author: sonnet
reason: A builds a clearer working model: its mode table, labelled diagram edges and explicit charge check show why exactly one engine charges and how a double charge is prevented at every mode change, including forward moves, which B never explains; B adds more edge-case detail, such as the stop point and reconciliation against the payment provider, but is longer and harder to take in.

author: haiku
reason: A explains the three rules the design follows, defines every term and status precisely, and gives a failure table showing what the customer sees and what happens to the cart in each case, so an outsider can understand both how the system works and why it works that way; B is shorter but leaves more to inference, such as an order id that also serves as the refund key, a coarser status model and less stated reasoning.

author: haiku
reason: B opens with a plain overview and the three rules that explain why the flow has this shape. It also defines the terms a newcomer would otherwise get stuck on (snapshot, valid hold, idempotency key, the separate order statuses), and ends with a failure table that answers "what happens if X breaks" at a glance, so it builds a better mental model than A even though A is tighter.
